summary:
Uber's managed software factory rests on six infrastructure layers. The Model Gateway is a single OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint with middleware for Spire identity, a data anonymizer redacting 20+ PII types, an AI guard running five safety models, caching, and token optimization, all under 100 ms. Every request is attributed to caller, team, and project; the gateway now serves 800+ projects at 100M+ model requests/day. The MCP Gateway crawls internal and SaaS APIs into MCP servers, normalizing auth and token exchange, and shifted to Omni MCP and then a CLI projection so responses stay out of context; a code-mode skill auto-generates Python for hot use cases, yielding 40%+ fleetwide token savings across 1,000+ tools. Dev pods were agentified into pre-provisioned Kubernetes balloon pods with snapshotted repos and pre-built search indices. The Skills Marketplace hosts 2,500 skills behind lint checks and automated review, with 20,000+ executions/day. The Context Graph unifies ~20-30 scattered ownership/dependency systems into 150 node/edge types and 40M entries. Cortana packages these layers across Slack, CLI, and web with personalized personas (300 in a month, 20k sessions/day).

Adam walks a World Cup stadium-pickup feature end-to-end: Cortana surfaces research and Figma mock-up variants, then hands off to Minion, Uber's cloud coding agent powered by dev pods with a full build environment. Minion deliberately stops at a draft PR to keep advanced validation in the inner loop before CI: visual validation launches a simulator, captures screenshots, and compares them to Figma specs; the service is brought up in backend staging to validate front-end/back-end integration. Static-analysis and lighter-model code review shift into the inner loop while a heavier reasoning skill powers outer-loop review and self-healing CI. PRs include a table of all checks, including screenshots, to give reviewers confidence. Maintenance runs as managed loops (e.g., feature-flag cleanup of the losing variant) scheduled for low-traffic windows, with landed/not-landed diff feedback improving skills and monthly incident reviews generating new maintenance skills. The closing bottleneck has moved from whether it can be built to whether it should be built, with CI capacity and experiment volume as new constraints.

sections.title: Opening and headline metrics
sections.summary: Uday and Adam introduce Uber's managed software factory journey. Headline metrics: 70%+ of PRs from agents, 2x lines of code per engineer YoY, 250 automated migrations covering 9M lines. Foundation: six years of monorepo and Bazel investment.

sections.title: Building block 1: Model Gateway with 100 ms guardrail budget
sections.summary: Model Gateway is a single OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint with Spire identity, 20+ PII-type redaction, an AI guard with five specialized safety models, caching, and token optimization—all under 100 ms. Attribution per caller/team/project enables spend views and guardrails; audit logs feed benchmarking. Serves 800+ projects at 100M+ model requests/day including frontier and open-source models.

sections.title: Building block 2: MCP Gateway and token tax reduction
sections.summary: MCP Gateway crawls internal APIs and SaaS tools into MCP servers, normalizing auth and token exchange. Token optimization moved from direct MCP to Omni MCP, then to CLI projection, plus a code-mode skill auto-generating Python for hot use cases. Result: 40%+ fleetwide token savings across 1,000+ tools.

sections.title: Building block 3: Agentified dev pods
sections.summary: Dev pods evolved into pre-provisioned Kubernetes balloon pods with snapshotted repos and pre-built search indices so agents start in seconds. A mega dev pod consolidates repos for cross-repo agent and engineer work, and non-engineers can spin up agent harnesses quickly.

sections.title: Building block 4: Managed skills marketplace
sections.summary: Engineers were duplicating skills with superpar quality. The marketplace now holds 2,500 skills behind lint checks, automated review, autoinstall by persona, and continuous evals feeding authors. 20,000+ skill executions/day run across the fleet.

sections.title: Building block 5: Context graph
sections.summary: Agents previously burned tokens across 20-30 systems for ownership and dependency context. The unified context graph encodes 150 node/edge types and 40M entries spanning mobile, backend, data lake, design docs, Jira, and incidents, dramatically improving tokens, turns, and latency for queries such as mobility cash trips in India.

sections.title: Building block 6: Cortana across Slack, CLI, and web
sections.summary: Cortana packages skills, MCPs, and the context graph across Slack, CLI, and web. Employees personalize with custom skills and prompts in team Slack channels. 300 unique personas were created in the last month with 20,000+ sessions/day.

sections.title: Adam's end-to-end feature walkthrough begins
sections.summary: Adam starts a feature from a Slack thread proposing better pickup locations near busy World Cup stadiums. The team tags Cortana, which uses the context graph to assess the business opportunity. He opens Cortana in a web interface showing research on past large-scale venue events and candidate stadiums, then turns to North America product requirements.

sections.title: Figma mock-ups, Minion hand-off, and draft PR
sections.summary: Cortana helps create initial Figma mock-ups with two button-string variants for an A/B experiment. Compressed design alignment that previously took weeks now produces a prototype quickly. The Cortana agent hands off to Minion, Uber's cloud coding agent powered by the dev pod building block, working across backend and frontend repos. Minion intentionally stops at a draft PR rather than pushing to CI, to avoid extra CI load and enable inner-loop validation of advanced end-to-end features before build queues.

sections.title: Inner-loop validation and outer-loop CI
sections.summary: Adam reframes the SDLC as inner loop and outer loop, shifting checks earlier. Inner loop runs static analysis and visual validation: a simulator launches, screenshots are captured and compared against Figma specs, and the service is brought up in backend staging to validate front-end/back-end integration. The outer loop runs CI, with self-healing CI fixing common issues, and code review using a powerful reasoning skill; parts of code review have moved into the inner loop using a faster medium model. Autonomous diffs from Minion attach a table summarizing all checks, including screenshots, so human reviewers see the full self-improvement history.

sections.title: Maintenance as a managed loop
sections.summary: With much more code flowing through the factory, maintenance matters more. Features and services can be enrolled in maintenance skills such as feature-flag cleanup—e.g., removing the losing World Cup modal B variant. These are centrally managed loops, not thousands of free-running ones, scheduled for low-traffic windows like Sunday and controlled so engineers aren't overwhelmed by diffs on Monday. Landed/not-landed diff comments serve as label data to improve the skills. At a monthly cadence, incident reviews surface new patterns that are turned into new maintenance skills applied across services.

sections.title: New bottlenecks: CI capacity, experiments, and what to build
sections.summary: Adam closes by pointing to other SDLC areas like monitoring that the building blocks can power, and to new bottlenecks emerging from increased agent output. Infrastructure strain is pushing the team to anticipate CI capacity needs and make foundational investments there. There are only so many experiments that can feasibly run. The biggest shift is decision-making: it is no longer whether they can build something but whether they should build it. Adam thanks the audience and tees up the next Uber talk on agentic code review.
